questions.question_text: Let $\alpha=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{16}+\dots\infty$ and $\beta=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{27}+\dots\infty$ . Then the value of $(0.2)^{log_{\sqrt{5}}(\alpha)}+(0.04)^{log_{5}(\beta)}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html:
Let $\alpha=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{16}+\dots\infty$ and

$\beta=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{27}+\dots\infty$ . Then the value of

$(0.2)^{log_{\sqrt{5}}(\alpha)}+(0.04)^{log_{5}(\beta)}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: We first find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ . Given $\alpha=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{16}+\cdot s$ This is an infinite geometric progression with $a=\frac{1}{4},r=\frac{1}{2}$ So, $\alpha=\frac{a}{1-r}=\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{1-\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$ Now, $\beta=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{27}+\cdot s$ This is also an infinite geometric progression with $a=\frac{1}{3},r=\frac{1}{3}$ Thus, $\beta=\frac{a}{1-r}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}}{1-\frac{1}{3}}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{2}{3}}=\frac{1}{2}$ So both are equal to $\frac{1}{2}$ . Now the expression becomes $(0.2)^{log_{\sqrt{5}}(\frac{1}{2})}+(0.04)^{log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})}$ Convert decimals into fractions: $0.2=\frac{1}{5},0.04=\frac{1}{25}=5^{-2}$ So, $(\frac{1}{5})^{log_{\sqrt{5}}(\frac{1}{2})}+(\frac{1}{25})^{log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})}$ That is, $5^{-log_{\sqrt{5}}(\frac{1}{2})}+5^{-2log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})}$ Now use the change of base idea: $log_{\sqrt{5}}(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})}{log_{5}(\sqrt{5})}$ Since $log_{5}(\sqrt{5})=log_{5}(5^{1/2})=\frac{1}{2}$ therefore $log_{\sqrt{5}}(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})}{1/2}=2log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})$ Hence first term: $5^{-log_{\sqrt{5}}(1/2)}=5^{-2log_{5}(1/2)}$ So both terms are same: $5^{-2log_{5}(1/2)}+5^{-2log_{5}(1/2)}=2 \cdot 5^{-2log_{5}(1/2)}$ Now use the identity $a^{log_{a}x}=x$ Then $5^{-2log_{5}(1/2)}=5^{log_{5}(1/2)^{-2}}\text{is not correct}$ So let us simplify properly: $-2log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})=log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})^{-2}?$ Instead, use $klog_{a}b=log_{a}(b^{k})$ Thus, $-2log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})=log_{5}((\frac{1}{2})^{-2})=log_{5}(4)$ Therefore, $5^{-2log_{5}(1/2)}=5^{log_{5}4}=4$ So the total value is $2 \times 4=8$ Hence, the required value is $8$ So the correct option is Option C .
questions.explanation_html:
We first find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ .

Given

$\alpha=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{16}+\cdot s$

This is an infinite geometric progression with

$a=\frac{1}{4},r=\frac{1}{2}$

So,

$\alpha=\frac{a}{1-r}=\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{1-\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$

Now,

$\beta=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{27}+\cdot s$

This is also an infinite geometric progression with

$a=\frac{1}{3},r=\frac{1}{3}$

Thus,

$\beta=\frac{a}{1-r}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}}{1-\frac{1}{3}}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{2}{3}}=\frac{1}{2}$

So both are equal to $\frac{1}{2}$ .

Now the expression becomes

$(0.2)^{log_{\sqrt{5}}(\frac{1}{2})}+(0.04)^{log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})}$

Convert decimals into fractions:

$0.2=\frac{1}{5},0.04=\frac{1}{25}=5^{-2}$

So,

$(\frac{1}{5})^{log_{\sqrt{5}}(\frac{1}{2})}+(\frac{1}{25})^{log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})}$

That is,

$5^{-log_{\sqrt{5}}(\frac{1}{2})}+5^{-2log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})}$

Now use the change of base idea:

$log_{\sqrt{5}}(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})}{log_{5}(\sqrt{5})}$

Since

$log_{5}(\sqrt{5})=log_{5}(5^{1/2})=\frac{1}{2}$

therefore

$log_{\sqrt{5}}(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})}{1/2}=2log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})$

Hence first term:

$5^{-log_{\sqrt{5}}(1/2)}=5^{-2log_{5}(1/2)}$

So both terms are same:

$5^{-2log_{5}(1/2)}+5^{-2log_{5}(1/2)}=2 \cdot 5^{-2log_{5}(1/2)}$

Now use the identity

$a^{log_{a}x}=x$

Then

$5^{-2log_{5}(1/2)}=5^{log_{5}(1/2)^{-2}}\text{is not correct}$

So let us simplify properly:

$-2log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})=log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})^{-2}?$

Instead, use

$klog_{a}b=log_{a}(b^{k})$

Thus,

$-2log_{5}(\frac{1}{2})=log_{5}((\frac{1}{2})^{-2})=log_{5}(4)$

Therefore,

$5^{-2log_{5}(1/2)}=5^{log_{5}4}=4$

So the total value is

$2 \times 4=8$

Hence, the required value is

$8$

So the correct option is Option C.

questions.question_text: The product of all solutions of the equation $e^{5(log_{e}x)^{2}+3}=x^{8},x>0$ , is :
questions.question_html: The product of all solutions of the equation $e^{5(log_{e}x)^{2}+3}=x^{8},x>0$ , is :
questions.explanation_text: We begin with the equation: $e^{5(log_{e}x)^{2}+3}=x^{8},x>0.$ Equating the exponents, we have: $5(log_{e}x)^{2}+3=log_{e}x^{8}=8log_{e}x.$ Let $t=log_{e}x$ . Substituting, the equation becomes: $5t^{2}+3=8t.$ Rewriting this as a quadratic equation: $5t^{2}-8t+3=0.$ Factoring the quadratic: $5t^{2}-5t-3t+3=0,$ $(5t-3)(t-1)=0.$ Thus, the solutions for $t$ are: $t=1$ implies $log_{e}x=1$ , giving $x=e$ . $t=\frac{3}{5}$ implies $log_{e}x=\frac{3}{5}$ , giving $x=e^{\frac{3}{5}}$ . The product of all solutions is: $e^{1} \times e^{\frac{3}{5}}=e^{1+\frac{3}{5}}=e^{\frac{8}{5}}.$
questions.explanation_html:
We begin with the equation:

$e^{5(log_{e}x)^{2}+3}=x^{8},x>0.$

Equating the exponents, we have:

$5(log_{e}x)^{2}+3=log_{e}x^{8}=8log_{e}x.$

Let $t=log_{e}x$ . Substituting, the equation becomes:

$5t^{2}+3=8t.$

Rewriting this as a quadratic equation:

$5t^{2}-8t+3=0.$

Factoring the quadratic:

$5t^{2}-5t-3t+3=0,$

$(5t-3)(t-1)=0.$

Thus, the solutions for $t$ are:

$t=1$ implies $log_{e}x=1$ , giving $x=e$ .

$t=\frac{3}{5}$ implies $log_{e}x=\frac{3}{5}$ , giving $x=e^{\frac{3}{5}}$ .

The product of all solutions is:

$e^{1} \times e^{\frac{3}{5}}=e^{1+\frac{3}{5}}=e^{\frac{8}{5}}.$

questions.question_text: If the solution of the equation $log_{cosx}cotx+4log_{sinx}tanx=1,x \in (0,\frac{\pi}{2})$ , is $sin^{-1}(\frac{\alpha+\sqrt{\beta}}{2})$ , where $\alpha$ , $\beta$ are integers, then $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: If the solution of the equation $log_{cosx}cotx+4log_{sinx}tanx=1,x \in (0,\frac{\pi}{2})$ , is $sin^{-1}(\frac{\alpha+\sqrt{\beta}}{2})$ , where $\alpha$ , $\beta$ are integers, then $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $log_{cosx}cotx+4log_{sinx}tanx=1$ $\Rightarrow log_{cosx}cotx-4log_{sinx}cotx=1$ $\Rightarrow 1-log_{cosx}sinx-4-4log_{sinx}cosx=1$ Let $log_{cosx}sinx=t$ $t+\frac{4}{t}=4$ $\Rightarrow t=2$ $sinx=cos^{2}x$ $\Rightarrow sinx=1-sin^{2}x$ $\Rightarrow sin^{2}x+sinx^{-1}=0$ $\Rightarrow sinx=\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$ as $x \in (0,\frac{\pi}{2})$ $sinx=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$ $x=sin^{-1}(\frac{-1+\sqrt{5}}{2})$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=-1,\beta=5$ $\alpha+\beta=4$
questions.explanation_html:
$log_{cosx}cotx+4log_{sinx}tanx=1$

$\Rightarrow log_{cosx}cotx-4log_{sinx}cotx=1$

$\Rightarrow 1-log_{cosx}sinx-4-4log_{sinx}cosx=1$

Let $log_{cosx}sinx=t$

$t+\frac{4}{t}=4$

$\Rightarrow t=2$

$sinx=cos^{2}x$

$\Rightarrow sinx=1-sin^{2}x$

$\Rightarrow sin^{2}x+sinx^{-1}=0$

$\Rightarrow sinx=\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$

as $x \in (0,\frac{\pi}{2})$

$sinx=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$

$x=sin^{-1}(\frac{-1+\sqrt{5}}{2})$

$\Rightarrow \alpha=-1,\beta=5$

$\alpha+\beta=4$

questions.question_text: The number of integral solutions $x$ of $log_{(x+\frac{7}{2})}(\frac{x-7}{2x-3})^{2} \ge 0$ is :
questions.question_html: The number of integral solutions $x$ of $log_{(x+\frac{7}{2})}(\frac{x-7}{2x-3})^{2} \ge 0$ is :
questions.explanation_html:
$log_{(x+\frac{7}{2})}(\frac{x-7}{2x-3})^{2} \ge 0$

Domain :

$\begin{aligned} & x+\frac{7}{2}>0 \\ \\ & x>\frac{-7}{2} \\ \\ & x+\frac{7}{2} \ne 1 \\ \\ & x \ne \frac{-5}{2} \\ \\ & \frac{x-7}{2x-3} \ne 0 \\ \\ & x \ne 7 \\ \\ & x \ne \frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$

$\text{Taking intersection :}x \in (\frac{-7}{2},\infty)-{-\frac{5}{2},\frac{3}{2},7}$

Now $log_{a}b \ge 0$ if $a>1$ and $b \ge 1$

$\begin{aligned} \text{Or} \\ \\ a \in (0,1)\text{and}b \in (0,1) \end{aligned}$

Case I : $x+\frac{7}{2}>1\text{and}(\frac{x-7}{2x-3})^{2} \ge 1$

$\therefore$ $x>-\frac{5}{2}$

and

$\begin{aligned} & (2x-3)^{2}-(x-7)^{2} \le 0 \\ \\ & (2x-3+x-7)(2x-3-x+7) \le 0 \\ \\ & (3x-10)(x+4) \le 0 \end{aligned}$

$x \in [-4,\frac{10}{3}]$

$\text{Intersection :}x \in (\frac{-5}{2},\frac{10}{3}]$

Case II : $x+\frac{7}{2} \in (0,1)\text{and}(\frac{x-7}{2x-3})^{2} \in (0,1)$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore 0<x+\frac{7}{2}<1 \\ \\ & -\frac{7}{2}<x<\frac{-5}{2} \end{aligned}$

and

$\begin{aligned} & (\frac{x-7}{2x-3})^{2}<1 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow (x-7)^{2}<(2x-3)^{2} \end{aligned}$

$\therefore$ $x \in (-\infty,-4)∪(\frac{10}{3},\infty)$

No common values of $x$ .

Hence intersection with feasible region.

We get $x \in (\frac{-5}{2},\frac{10}{3}]-{\frac{3}{2}}$

Integral value of $x$ are ${-2,-1,0,1,2,3}$

No. of integral values $=6$

questions.question_text: The number of solutions of the equation log 4 (x $-$ 1) = log 2 (x $-$ 3) is _________.
questions.question_html: The number of solutions of the equation log4(x $-$ 1) = log2(x $-$ 3) is _________.
questions.explanation_text: $log_{4}(x-1)=log_{2}(x-3)$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}log_{2}(x-1)=log_{2}(x-3)$ $\Rightarrow log_{2}(x-1)^{1/2}=log_{2}(x-3)$ $\Rightarrow (x-1)^{1/2}=log_{2}(x-3)$ $\Rightarrow (x-1)^{1/2}=x-3$ $\Rightarrow x-1=x^{2}+9-6x$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}-7x+10=0$ $\Rightarrow (x-2)(x-5)=0$ $\Rightarrow x=2,5$ But x $\ne$ 2 because it is not satisfying the domain of given equation i.e. log 2 (x $-$ 3) $\rightarrow$ its domain x > 3 finally x is 5 $\therefore$ No. of solutions = 1.
questions.explanation_html:
$log_{4}(x-1)=log_{2}(x-3)$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}log_{2}(x-1)=log_{2}(x-3)$

$\Rightarrow log_{2}(x-1)^{1/2}=log_{2}(x-3)$

$\Rightarrow (x-1)^{1/2}=log_{2}(x-3)$

$\Rightarrow (x-1)^{1/2}=x-3$

$\Rightarrow x-1=x^{2}+9-6x$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}-7x+10=0$

$\Rightarrow (x-2)(x-5)=0$

$\Rightarrow x=2,5$

But x $\ne$ 2 because it is not satisfying the domain of given equation i.e. log2(x $-$ 3) $\rightarrow$ its domain x > 3

finally x is 5

$\therefore$ No. of solutions = 1.
